To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
all four Fat paralogs are transcriptionally down-regulated in the cerebellar cortex of the DplQ71 mice, and that conditional KO of Fat 3 in the brain does not affect autophagy.

1) Fat3 is widely expressed in the mouse brain; 2) conditional KO of Fat 3 in the brain of adult mice does not lead to any behavioral or biochemical abnormalities; 3) Fat3 does not appear to be required for normal autophagy.
Fat3 is the most widely expressed fat homologue in the brain, and that conditional KO of Fat in the brain has no effect on autophagy or behavior.

the transcriptional downregulation and potential role of Fat3 in neurodegenerative diseases.
the role of Fat cadherins in neurodegenerative mouse models.
the role of Fat3 in autophagy in the mouse brain, with the aim of providing a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Fat orthologues in mice do not play any major role in autophagy and neurodegeneration in the mouse model of DRPDLA.
Fat3 is not involved in the pathogenesis of the DRPLA mouse model.
Fat3 is not required for normal brain development or function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the downregulation of Fat3 is not a cause of neurodegeneration in DRPLA mice.
the downregulation of Fat orthologues in mouse models of DRPLA does not appear to be a cause of neurodegeneration, but may rather be an adaptive response to stress.
Fat3 KO in the brain of mice does not affect autophagy or neurodegeneration, at least under the conditions of our study.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Fat3 is expressed in the brain and is transcriptionally downregulated during DRPLA.
Fat3 is not a good candidate for the study of neurodegeneration in mouse models of DRPLA, and this may apply to other neurodegenerative diseases as well.
Fat3 is not involved in neurodegeneration in a mouse model for DRPLA.
